transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Voters gave control of Congress to Democrats in this week's midterm elections.
The Democrats will take power next year.
Some races are still outstanding, including two Senate campaigns, one in Alaska and another
in Mississippi.
A top issue is affordability.
NPR's Willa Rubin says one pressing item is how lawmakers could deal with energy prices.
Congress can limit funding for the war.
They control the purse strings, after all.
They can hold back confirmations of new officials, pass resolutions.
But remember, the president has veto power, and in recent weeks, he's sent mixed signals
about whether he's going to escalate the war or end it.
Now, there are some things that the president and Congress might all be able to get behind.
One idea the president floated this spring was to temporarily waive the federal gas tax.
And the current Congress has introduced several bills to that effect.
But waiving that tax would be small savings, about 18 cents a gallon.
And it would mean less money to do things like repair roads.
NPR's Willa Rubin reporting.
After Democrats won full control of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, California
Congressman Robert Garcia is set to become the next chair of the House Oversight Committee.
He is promising to look into funding for President Trump's immigration enforcement operations.
NPR's Jasmine Garz has more.
The current Congress basically gave immigration enforcement a blank check.
In 2025 and 2026, Congress gave around $240 billion, that's billion with a B, to ICE and
Customs and Border Patrol.
Now, the incoming Congress, which just got voted in, could stop giving them even more
money.
So the truth is ICE and DHS have gotten enough funds to run mass deportation operations for
the remainder of Trump's term.
NPR's Jasmine Garz reporting.
Authorities in Wisconsin say that an infant has died of measles.
It's part of a large ongoing outbreak of the disease.
NPR's Maria Godoy reports on the third measles-associated death reported in the U.S. this week.
Wisconsin health officials say measles was the immediate cause of death of the baby,
whose age was not disclosed.
Infants younger than six months cannot receive the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine.
The state has reported 431 measles cases across 13 counties this year, though the true number
is likely much higher.
Earlier this week, New York officials announced that an unvaccinated child in a rural part
of the state had died as part of its measles outbreak.
Meanwhile, in neighboring Pennsylvania, which is battling the country's worst measles outbreak
in more than three decades, health officials confirmed the state's six measles-associated
death.
Measles is highly contagious, and vaccination remains the best protection.
Maria Godoy, NPR News.
This is NPR News.
There's been a major political development in the Kurdistan region of Iraq.
One of two main political parties has announced it is withdrawing from the regional government.
NPR's Jane Arav reports it is threatening to form a breakaway administration.
The Kurdistan region is part of Iraq, but it's semi-autonomous, and it has its own
parliament.
The two main political parties control different parts of the region, and they've long been
rivals.
The head of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, Balfour Talibani, announced his party was
withdrawing from the regional government after a two-year-long dispute over government posts.
He threatened to create a separate administration in areas his party controls.
Tensions are already high due to continued attacks by Iran, which is targeting armed
Iranian Kurdish opposition groups in Iraq's Kurdistan region, and following the withdrawal
of U.S. forces from Iraq in September.
Jane Arav, NPR News, Amman.
In the U.S., the federal government says that hiring soared in October.
The Labor Department reports employers created 165,000 new jobs last month.
That's far more than economic analysts had expected.
The industries that saw the biggest growth were in health care, transportation, and in
professional services.
There were also increases in the average wages that Americans earned.
These wages were up 3.1 percent, but it is not clear yet if those gains are enough to
keep up with inflation.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Democrats win control of Congress in midterm elections; Alaska and Mississippi Senate races still outstanding
NPR's Willa Rubin reports on Congress's options to limit war funding and address energy prices, including a federal gas tax waiver
Robert Garcia set to chair House Oversight Committee, promising scrutiny of ICE and immigration enforcement funding
Wisconsin reports infant measles death amid large statewide outbreak of 431 cases
Maria Godoy reports on measles deaths in Wisconsin, New York, and Pennsylvania, the nation's worst outbreak in decades
Patriotic Union of Kurdistan leader Bafel Talabani withdraws from Kurdistan regional government, threatens breakaway administration
Labor Department reports employers added 165,000 jobs in October, well above expectations, with wages up 3.1%
